title: Flagey Building, Brussels
lede: Joseph Diongre’s broadcasting house for Belgian radio, nicknamed the paquebot for its ship-like silhouette: curved facades of ribbon windows and a round tower.
summary: A curved pale yellow block with continuous ribbon windows and a round banded tower. Joseph Diongre, Ixelles, 1933–38.

evidence.note: Downloaded to a scratch folder and inspected Busoni’s 2013 photograph on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ancien_Institut_national_de_Radiodiffusion_-_vue_d%27ensemble.JPG) at 1280 px. No image is stored.

styles.note: A European paquebot building: curved facades, horizontal bands of windows, and a round tower like a ship’s funnel.

context: Joseph Diongre won a 1933 competition and the building was completed in 1938 as the headquarters of the National Institute of Radio Broadcasting (INR/NIR). Wikipedia calls it Streamline Moderne and gives the nickname “paquebot” (packet boat). Studio 4 is a noted concert hall. It is now the Flagey cultural centre. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagey_Building).
observed: A six-storey block with a pale yellow facade curves around the corner of the square in one continuous sweep.
Every floor has a continuous ribbon of windows separated by solid horizontal bands of the yellow wall, so the facade reads as stacked horizontal stripes.
A round tower rises from the curved corner; each of its floors is a ring of windows under a projecting band, and a lantern and mast sit on top.
Small round clocks sit on the facade near the top of the curve. The walls carry no applied ornament.
interpretation: Flagey shows a European version of the style: no chrome and no portholes, but curved corners, continuous horizontal bands, and a funnel-like tower make the ship reading.
borrow: Wrap a corner with one continuous curve and let horizontal bands run unbroken around it.
A stack of rings with projecting edges reads as a streamline tower or a progress indicator.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Joseph Diongre died in 1963, so the building is protected in Belgium until 2033. Belgian freedom of panorama would probably permit exterior photographs, and the Commons photograph is CC BY-SA 3.0; the lead curator can decide whether to upgrade.
